title: Build context-aware agents: From data to decisions | BRK240

segments.text: Amanda Silver: Welcome, everyone, to Build.
I'm Amanda Silver, and I'm joined
with my friend here, Marco Casalaina.
Marco Casalaina: Hello, I'm Marco Casalaina.
Amanda Silver: So I've spent more than two decades working
at Microsoft on developer tools and platforms,
and I've really never, ever seen a shift as profound as the one
that we're going through now.
What we're seeing is that software is evolving
from people-driven applications to agents that are defined
by intent, and they're measured by the outcomes.
And so these agents can reason, they can retrieve context,
they can make decisions,
they can take action on a user's behalf.
And in many ways, this is really the automated future
that we've all been working towards for decades.
But there's a problem.
More than 40% of agentic AI projects are expected to fail.
And that's not because the models aren't capable,
but it's because the agents lack the context that they need
to be able to succeed.
And so to make it work, developers actually have
to stitch together the fragmented data sources,
the custom retrieval systems, the permissions models,
the orchestration logic, just to make agents useful.
And we're all really figuring this out together,
so we're all learning from each other.
We don't necessarily know what the best practices are.
But the result is that the experiences are brittle
for the end user.
And we see agents that hallucinate.
We see systems that miss policy boundaries.
And they break when they're deployed into production.
And the challenge isn't giving agents the access to information.
It's giving them a shared understanding of the people
and the data and the policies and the business context
that surround the agents as they're doing their work.
So when a team actually gets this right,
when organizations get this right, everything changes.
The agents stop acting like isolated apps,
and they start operating with an understanding of the enterprise
around them, the people, the data,
the workflows, and the policies.
And the result is that the agents have better accuracy.
They are more reliable actions.
There's dramatically less engineering that you need to put
into building these agents.
And you don't have to recreate the context
for every single agent that you build.
It's really kind of the difference.
The way I think about it is the difference
between welcoming a brand-new employee to the team
versus somebody who's actually a seasoned employee on your team.
So the question is, how can you take that knowledge
that a seasoned employee has and infuse every new agent
with that context as they're executing?
So this is how we think about Microsoft IQ.
You can think about IQ
as the context layer for the agentic web.
It brings together four different sources of context.
Work IQ for the organizational context,
Fabric IQ for the business knowledge, Foundry IQ for all
of the enterprise knowledge and policies,
and Web IQ for the world's knowledge.
And together, the system really gives agents a shared
understanding of the world, of your business,
of the work that's happening on your teams.
And this is what enables the agents to have enough context
to make the right decision, to take the right actions,
and to achieve the outcomes that you are trying to get them
to achieve so that you can trust them.
So let's jump into a demo really quickly.
I want to show you what it looks like in practice.
Last week, I sent Marco an email with an idea, a crazy idea.
There was no spec, just an email, no design doc.
And so he's going to show you how he went
from that to a working agent.
Marco Casalaina: All right. Thank you, Amanda.
All right. So here it is.
This is the email that Amanda sent to me.
So we have this onerous refund process,
and she thought it might be a good idea to make an agent
to do this stuff with all the different IQs.
Now I am going to start with Work IQ.
So here I am in Copilot CLI,
and it does have a handy-dandy voice mode over here.
So I think it's control+xv.
Amanda Silver sent me an email about this refund agent idea.
Let's start to make a plan, a little spec for this thing
so we can build this agent.
Go look up that email.
All right.
So, what's going to happen here in a moment is
that I have Work IQ installed into my Copilot CLI.
What it's going to do here, it is going to use Work IQ
to go find that email.
In this case, I am using,
or really it's using Work IQ on my behalf.
I've authorized it on my behalf.
Or it might have a transient error.
But that happens.
That's all good.
Okay. So anyway.
Amanda Silver: There we go.
Marco Casalaina: Well, maybe not.
I actually had it preloaded in a tab somewhere, but okay.
So we're going to get a transient error.
Suffice it to say that with Work IQ,
it can log in on your behalf.
And in fact, if you use M365 Copilot,
that is also what it's doing.
You'll notice that for those of you who use Copilot,
when you use it, there's a little thing at the top
that says Work IQ, and it's using Work IQ
to look up your email.
Now, in any case, with that, we did make a spec.
And so here is the spec that we ended up with.
And with this spec, we ended
up actually building the agent itself.
And this is the agent.
Now, this agent is using-- this is the front end,
the fancy front end for the agent, but if we look at it
in Foundry, this is what this agent actually looks like.
And in this agent, we are using all four of the IQs.
And so, Amanda, if you don't mind,
maybe you could tell us a little bit about Web IQ and Foundry IQ.
Amanda Silver: Sure. Sounds good.
Okay. So, it didn't work.
We're going to come back to Work IQ.
Maybe Marco can actually go and debug it so we make sure
that the Work IQ works for our later demo.
But basically what we want to see now is
that we can actually have Work IQ kind of work
in combination with Web IQ.
And so what I want to kind of talk
about here is really what is Web IQ.
In a sense, the agents don't just need
to understand your business.
Oftentimes what they need to understand is the real world
in which your business is operating.
I was talking with somebody today
who delivers consumer goods, and he really needs
to understand the micro events, the local events
that are happening, so that he can actually have micro
targeting of his different consumer goods that he's trying
to deliver to all of these different markets.
So that's a great example
of where you might use something like Web IQ.
So Web IQ really connects AI
to authoritative real-world information.
It's a structured multimodal index across the web, news,
images, and video so that agents can be grounded--
and have their responses grounded
in fresh, verifiable context.
It's not a traditional search API that's wrapped in AI.
It's actually a grounding platform that's built
specifically for the needs of modern agentic systems.
So if you think about building agents at scale,
three things really matter.
First quality.
Web IQ delivers structured, citation-ready results
across the web, news, images, video,
and it helps the agents generate the answers
that users can verify and trust.
Second speed.
Agent workflows are inherently multi-step.
And so retrieval and reasoning and planning
and action, they all add latency.
So with sub-200 millisecond P95 grounding,
Web IQ really helps keep those workflows responsive even
as the agents chain together multiple operations.
And the third thing we have to think about is efficiency.
The context windows are really valuable real estate.
So Web IQ uses the passage-level ranking
to surface the highest signal information while filtering
out the noise, that allows you to reduce the token consumption
and lowering the overall costs of the agents
that are operating at scale.
So Web IQ is already being used by frontier model providers
and a bunch of enterprises, and it's available today
for a few Azure customers.
One example is NASDAQ.
So they have this solution they call Boardvantage,
and NASDAQ really helps boards and executives make decisions
in real time where the accuracy, the timelines,
and the trust are really critical.
And so that means that they can bring together the enterprise
information and all of the external signals
that they can get on the web without having
to compromise the security or the data boundaries.
So with Web IQ, NASDAQ can actually ground the AI
in this fresh, authoritative information
so that they can make all of these decisions in real time.
And the result is faster access to the external context,
higher quality responses, and a simpler architecture
that allows them to build AI applications.
So next up is Foundry IQ.
So if Web IQ connects agents to the world's knowledge,
Foundry IQ connects them to your knowledge.
Enterprise knowledge, you can think about it as all
of that context that is scattered throughout your
organization, in data platforms, in content repositories,
in business systems, in your custom applications.
Now, today, developers have
to spend too much time stitching all
of these sources together before an agent can actually deliver
the value.
But Foundry IQ changes that.
It provides the unified knowledge layer
that automatically ingests and enriches,
and it connects the enterprise information,
and it eliminates a bunch of the retrieval logic
and infrastructure that you would have to build otherwise.
And then at runtime, when the agent is operating,
Foundry IQ intelligently retrieves the right information
for you and from the right sources,
giving the agents the context that they need
to answer accurately and enable the agent to act confidently.
So that means less infrastructure that you have
to manage and more intelligence
for the agents that you're building.
So here's the mental model for Foundry IQ.
At the foundation are your knowledge sources,
your enterprise data, your documents,
your applications, and the live web.
And above that is the context layer, where memory, embeddings,
and the semantic models all turn
that information into understanding.
And then at the top are the agents and the applications
that the users interact with.
So the key idea here is delegation.
Every layer does one thing really well.
Knowledge sources, they store the information.
And the agents retrieve it and reason
over it, and they take action.
And as a developer, you don't want to have to rebuild
that machinery inside every single agent.
You might want to define a knowledge base
that you then make available
to multiple agents throughout your organization.
So you want to build on top of it so that you can get
to your solution faster.
But great grounding isn't just about the retrieval.
It's also about trust.
So that's why security, and governance,
and policy enforcement are built directly into the platform,
not bolted on afterwards.
And today, we're actually introducing a new serverless
developer tier that gives every developer an easy way
to get started building with Foundry IQ and allows them
to scale to production when they're ready.
Now, several organizations are already using Foundry IQ.
Sitecore, which is a leader in digital experience
and content management.
It's a great example of what this looks like in practice.
Foundry IQ gives them reusable knowledge bases,
agentic retrieval,
and enterprise-grade security out of the box.
And Sitecore took those capabilities
and then applied them directly to a real business problem
so that they could make sure that their marketing
and their brand knowledge is accessible to every agent
across their organization every time,
with all the right permissions.
So that's exactly why we built Foundry IQ,
so that developers can plug in their existing workflows
and immediately empower the agents to be more accurate,
more grounded, governed, and ready for production deployment.
So now let's bring it all together.
Marco is going to show you now what happens
when you connect our refund agent to both Web IQ
and Foundry IQ, and grounding it in the real-world information,
the enterprise knowledge
that you have inside your organization,
and the governance required for production.
So you'll see the knowledge base come online,
the agent retrieves the context that it needs, and the policies
that will ensure that it operates safely in production.
Over to you, Marco.
Marco Casalaina: Or we like to think that that'll happen.
But in the time that you've been talking up there, I discovered
that my network has gone down hard.
So we're going to make do with what we got here
and hope for the best.
So now we talked about Web IQ.
Now we have, as I said, we grounded this agent
to all four of the IQs.
Now with Web IQ, that allows us to ground
to real-time world data.
Now in this case, I'm asking--
this is our package delivery system
and refunds and things like that.
And I am asking it about the Sandy Fire.
The Sandy Fire is, right now, still burning 400 miles south
of here in Simi Valley.
And so the idea would be, if my network were working,
that it will very quickly go to Web IQ and get back this result
and ground this agent to the real-time data.
But I'm not going to sit here and wait for that to come back,
because that doesn't seem to be working.
I even tried hotspotting it to my phone.
Not great.
So we're going to make do with what we got.
Now, I am also linking this to Foundry IQ.
So you see I got my Foundry IQ over here.
What's that all about?
So here is Foundry IQ with plenty of little errors
on top due to my lack of a network connection.
But what is not a problem here is the fact
that I have connected this to a bunch of different data sources.
And this highlights one of the key aspects
of what these IQs are all about, and that is reuse.
The fact is, I got-- let's see, how many agents have I got in here?
I got 35 agents in here, of which 31 are currently running.
And I'm connecting a bunch of them to the same data sources.
I'm grounding them to the same context.
And so what I don't want to do is redefine this over, and over,
and over again, for every single agent that I build.
And so instead what I can do is use a Foundry IQ knowledge base.
Now, it's a little bit of a misnomer
to call it a knowledge base
because that's not really what Foundry IQ is.
What it really is, is a separate sub-agent.
This is doing agentic retrieval, and that means
that it can try and try again.
It can re-rank results before it gives it
up to my downstream agent.
And so it can search through all these things,
and it reduces the amount of challenge that I have.
He's giving me a new network connection over here;
I'll take that in a minute, not right now.
Anyway, all right.
So, basically this allows me to reuse this context
across multiple different agents.
And so with that, Amanda, maybe we can talk a little bit about--
now you see, also we're using here Foundry IQ--
sorry, Fabric IQ in the form of the Fabric data agent.
And why don't you tell a little bit
about Fabric IQ while I attempt to repair my network?
Amanda Silver: Go, go, Marco.
We're all rooting for you, man.
All right.
So Foundry IQ really helps you unlock all of the information
that your organization knows.
But Fabric IQ is what helps them understand what's happening
in real time.
It allows the agents to connect to the data that you have
in your organization, the metrics, the semantic models,
and reports that describe the current state of the business
so that they can reason with the same context that people use
to make decisions across your team every day.
So there are really three different outcomes
that it can deliver.
A shared understanding of how the business operates,
insights that can turn those into actions,
and agents that can reason over the business context,
not just the raw data.
But what really is it?
At the foundation, there's all of your unified data in OneLake.
So no matter where your data is today, even if it's not
in a Microsoft database, you can actually bring it into OneLake.
And it can kind of reason over it.
You can have semantic models that are modeling all
of your business metrics.
Now, most of you have probably already defined these
in Power BI.
And one of the things that's so incredible about Fabric IQ is
that it can just pick up what you've already defined
in Power BI and start enabling the agents to reason over it.
And then the ontologies,
they capture what your business really means.
All of the entities, and the relationships, and the rules,
and the constraints that your business operates on.
So all three of those layers live in Fabric,
and they're co-located with the data that they describe.
They're not stitched together as you're trying to assemble it.
So let's first talk about OneLake.
You can think about it as a single unified data layer
for your organization, and it brings together the analytical
and operational data across the systems and the clouds
that you're working in without having
to constantly move it or duplicate it.
And that really matters because agents are only as good
as the data that they can access.
But with OneLake, every team, every application,
and every agent can work from the same source of truth.
And that eliminates all of the silos and all
of the re-authentication and all of the authentication errors
that you have to deal with.
And it allows these AI systems to have consistent, scalable,
and cost-effective solutions here.
Now, on top of OneLake are these semantic models.
And they are what bridge the gap between the data
and the business meaning.
And they define the metrics and the concepts that the orgs,
that your teams use to run your business.
Now, that way, when an agent asks what happened,
it gets the same answer that your Power BI solution,
your Power BI dashboards,
are going to deliver what your analysts see,
and ultimately what you report up to your executives as well.
Now, ontologies, this is what gives the live model
of the business.
It's the entities, and the relationships, and the rules,
and the processes for your organization.
Now, that means that the agents can actually reason
about the customers and the orders, not just the tables
and the schemas, and the rows.
And you can bootstrap an ontology
from your existing semantic models.
Or you can create one from scratch, obviously.
But this is what gives agents the native understanding
of how your organization operates.
Now, Hanwha Qcells manages energy for AI data centers,
and they have a problem that is increasingly too dynamic
and complex for humans to really reason about on their own.
So they've used Fabric IQ to build an operational model
of the data center that's understood by people,
applications, but also by these AI agents.
And that common understanding is what allows the agents to reason
about the business, the recommended actions,
and continuously optimize the operations,
all while keeping human operators in control.
And it doesn't replace human judgment,
but it allows the agents to automate,
given the context of the business.
All right. How are we doing, Marco?
Marco Casalaina: I think we're going
to have to make do. It'll be fine.
Amanda Silver: Okay, okay, okay.
So what we're going to show you now is how the refund agent can
be grounded in the knowledge
from Fabric IQ using the ontology
and the semantic models that we had defined.
So let's see if Marco can show us what we're talking about.
Marco Casalaina: I'm going to do the best I can.
I don't know, man.
He came out, he gave me a new network,
and it still doesn't work, so I don't know.
Maybe my computer just doesn't want to connect today.
Fortunately, I preloaded a lot of this stuff in case
such a thing happened, and it did.
So here we have it.
Now, here's the deal.
Amanda Silver: It brings me back to the old days
of when the cloud was really flaky, and we had to do demos,
and we had to cache every single web page.
So thank you, Marco.
Marco Casalaina: It could be worse,
right? At least it didn't blue screen.
All right, anyway.
[ Laughter ]
All right.
So here's the deal.
We got all this data in our OneLake catalog,
all this structured data.
And I, as a human, this is how I access the data.
I'll make all these Power BI reports.
But what I'm not going to do, I'm not going
to give Power BI reports to my agents.
That doesn't make any sense.
I don't know why we would do that.
So we need something better for our agents.
Now, underneath these Power BI reports is a semantic model.
And the semantic model tells the system what the relationships
are between all of the tables.
So you've got our packages and our drivers.
And you see the one-to-many's.
And that's almost, almost what an agent needs, but not quite,
because it kind of tells it about what the relationships are
between these tables and stuff,
but it doesn't really tell it what it means, like what it is.
So fortunately, now we got this button
over here called "Generate Ontology."
And if I were to press it, I expect that nothing will happen
because I've got no network right now, but I'm going
to press it anyway, just for the feeling, yeah.
So as I expected--
[ Laughter ]
-- nothing, nothing.
But under normal circumstances,
we would see an ontology generator screen over here
that would get me started
in generating this ontology, which I did do.
So here is the ontology over here.
And I probably won't be able to show you too much about this.
But what I will say is.
Now, if you look at this, this is one portion
of my ontology that I built.
This is the part about the packages
and the customers and things like that.
And in a way, it kind of looks
like the semantic model, but it's not.
It's different.
Because these things--
in an ontology, these things are not tables.
These are business entities.
These are things that matter to your business.
And these relationships between them,
these are not necessarily table relationships.
These are verbs.
A customer can send or receive a package.
A package can be sent to a customer.
And that's what forms the relationships
in these ontologies.
You can also add to these things, and I'm not even going
to try to show this right now.
You can also add additional metadata,
additional semantics to this.
So, for example, what is a package to us?
What do we consider to be a package?
What are some synonyms?
I might call it a box or a case or a shipment
or something like that.
And so if I'm interacting with this data,
I might use any of these words.
And this ontology helps the agent convert those words
to what is underneath the scenes, a query.
And so the ontology allows me to give these semantics to my table
to tell the agents what that is all about.
Now you can use an ontology directly as an MCP server.
So when you define an ontology, there is an MCP server
that you can then connect to, or anyway connect your agents
to that will allow them to use that ontology.
You can also do it here in Fabric IQ.
I'm sorry, in Foundry IQ.
So you can actually connect Foundry IQ
to a Fabric ontology as well.
And that really, what it's doing, it's connected
to the MCP server also.
So it's using that ontology as a data source.
Now, in this case, I'm going to, just for the sake of--
just for sillies, I'm going to reload this page again just
to see if it wants to come back.
Because if you look closely at the way that I set
up this thing, I actually did not connect it just directly
to the ontology.
And the reason is, well, you're not going to be able to see it
because it's not going to want to come up.
So I connected it instead to a Fabric data agent.
So the Fabric data agent is a separate agent.
And with the Fabric data agent, I can actually connect
to a whole bunch of different data sources.
So this Fabric data agent
that you totally can't see is connected to the ontology,
but also to a lakehouse and to some other sources.
In that Fabric data agent, I have lots of context.
So there's the semantics coming from the ontology itself.
But I also have a lot of semantics
that I added about the lakehouse.
Because the second real purpose of all
of these IQs is what I call context delegation.
Every agent like this is sitting on top of a model.
And every model has a finite context.
There's only so much that you can put
in your agent's head, so to speak.
To query any structured data source
like a lakehouse requires tons and tons of context.
You've got to give it what is each data source.
You've got to give it the data dictionary for each data source.
You have to give it example queries.
Here's how you query this thing.
And you also have to give it ancillary instructions,
like in my data agent, if only I could show it to you,
in my data agent, I got a bunch of acronyms.
So I got an acronym in there called SRC,
Shipping Refund Concession,
which is specific only to this business.
So it's not going to be in the data.
It's not going to be in the data dictionary.
The model's going to have no idea what an SRC is.
So the only way that it would know what this term is,
is if we tell it, if we define it.
And this is a lot of what you're doing
when you're developing agents today.
You're inputting this sort of tribal knowledge,
this information that is in your head.
What is an SRC?
Well, now it knows.
And so we put all of that context
into the Fabric data agent so I don't have to put it in here.
So I don't have to define
that in every single agent that I have.
We export that knowledge so that
when it needs this structured data, it doesn't need
to keep all that context in its head.
Instead, it phones a friend.
It calls the Fabric data agent to get that data.
Now, let's take it away and bring it back to Work IQ.
Meanwhile, I'll continue fiddling with the network.
Maybe we'll get it back.
Amanda Silver: Okay. Do we have videos?
Marco Casalaina: (Inaudible)
Amanda Silver: We can always bring those up, too.
Okay. Marco really used Work IQ in act 1, or he was supposed
to have, if he could have connected to the network,
to basically take my email and turn that into a plan
that he then implemented that application
that he showed you a second ago.
Now, let's talk about Work IQ specifically.
It's really kind of-- you could think about it
as the people layer of Microsoft IQ.
What it does is it basically takes all of the context
of what your organization knows.
Now, what does your organization know?
It knows what you guys converse, you discuss over email
or what you discuss over Teams.
And it basically takes all of that context, all of the data
that lives in M365, and it allows the agent to be imbued
with that knowledge so that it can understand your business
processes, your collaboration, who is involved in a project,
what's important, what decisions have already been made,
what needs the attention next.
Because the most valuable context
in an organization isn't just data.
It's actually the people.
It's the people that are collaborating, that are working
across the team to get everything over the finish line.
So what makes IQ different than, say, the graph or kind
of more any traditional APIs historically?
Three things.
First, it's built for agents, not users.
If you think about the way that APIs,
traditional applications might access the graph
or an API before, that would be on the scale of a human, right?
What is the interactivity that a human needs?
This is really designed to support the speed
that an agentic process would need.
It's also built around the organizational context,
not the raw data.
And it's built on top of your existing security model.
It's not a copy of it.
So all of the Work IQ data stays
in your M365 context and in that tenant.
And so that means that developers don't have
to build their own systems that index all of this information.
They don't have to extract all of the data from their M365.
They don't have to build their own retrieval pipelines
or their own governance layer just
to help the agents have the context that all
of their other employees have.
It allows the agents to just get the work done.
And Work IQ is what provides that foundation out of the box.
Now, it's really built for this agent-first world.
So traditional APIs, they were built
around applications and users.
Work IQ is designed around agents, these systems that need
to reason and retrieve the context and collaborate
and take action across the organization.
And it brings together four different capabilities
into a single intelligence layer.
First is Chat.
Chat enables the agents to interact with the people
and other agents, supporting these conversational experiences
that you might get in Microsoft Copilot
with agent-to-agent collaboration.
The context gives the agents the grounded understanding
of what's happening across the organization,
drawing from the emails, the meetings, the chat, Teams chats,
documents, conversations, workflows, without having
to require the developers
to build their own retrieval orchestration process
or their own index.
The tools provide the capabilities, the simplified
and governed way for agents to retrieve that information,
but also to take action just as any other user would
in the context of M365.
So they can send an email.
They can send a message.
And all of that can be used via any kind
of agent-friendly service.
And then last, I think this is really interesting,
is workspaces.
What are workspaces?
They're these-- the persistent place for the agents
to actually work to kind
of store their intermediate work product
as they're getting things done.
So if you think about agents are becoming increasingly more
longer-running tasks.
They need to maintain state.
They need to be able to share their progress
across different phases of the plan that they're executing
with other agents that they might be collaborating with
or with humans that they're collaborating with.
So all of these capabilities together,
these are what give the organizations the same--
I mean, give the agents the same organizational context
that an employee has on your team.
So Miro is a good example
of a partner who's been integrating with Work IQ.
And they're basically integrating all
of the context directly into the collaborative experience
for their application as well.
So instead of copying the information between the tools
or working from stale snapshots,
the teams can actually access the same Microsoft 365 context
and the documents, the conversations, all of the people
that they need to collaborate with, all of those decisions.
But they can now access it directly from the Miro canvas.
So there's no copy-paste that has to be done.
There's no disconnected tools.
There's no stale information
when Miro is connecting to this environment.
It's just this shared context that seamlessly flows from M365
into Miro and vice versa.
Now, that's exactly the kind of connected experience
